Issued at 319 AM CDT Thu Sep 3 2026

Through Today...

Per an early morning hand surface analysis, a stationary front 
extends across southern Minnesota, southern Wisconsin, southern
Lower Michigan, and into northern New York. Quasi-zonal flow 
remains atop the front between a slow-moving upper-level low now
in western Quebec and a stalled upper-level high centered over 
the southeastern United States. Along and south of the front, it
remains balmy with current temperatures and dew points in the 
low to mid 70s. 

Per regional VWPs and RAP-analyzed mesoanalysis data, a broad 
low-level jet arcs from the southern Plains toward the middle 
Mississippi River Valley. Showers and thunderstorms are 
increasing in coverage at the nose of the jet near the Iowa and 
Minnesota border at press time. A gradual increase in ACCAS 
across central Wisconsin hints that additional development may 
soon take place in the vicinity of the stationary front, as 
well. At this point, all indications are that any convective 
development through mid-morning will either lift northeastward 
toward or remain tied to the stationary front to our north. 
Accordingly, today is shaping up to be another hot and humid 
day across the area.

Even with modest mixing today, will continue to incorporate 
typically moist guidance (NAM3/HRDPS) for dew points given 
continued impacts of evapotranspiration and even modest pooling 
ahead of composite outflow emanating from the north (more on 
that shortly). When paired with high temperatures in the mid to 
locally upper 90s, heat index values should rise back into the 
100 to 105F range by early afternoon across much of the area 
again. To have three days in a row with heat index above 100 in 
our area in September is relatively uncommon. 

Unfortunately, forecast confidence lowers by mid-afternoon 
owing to mixed signals in both regional observations and model 
guidance for the development and coverage of thunderstorms later
this evening. Conceptually speaking, would expect thunderstorm 
coverage to increase in southern Wisconsin at some point this 
afternoon which should send a push of relatively cool outflow 
southward (by way of crossing the state line and/or moving 
onshore from Lake Michigan). With the very moist and unstable 
airmass in place across our region, can also envision 
thunderstorms developing along or just ahead of the southward- 
moving outflow across our area, as well. The time at which this 
outflow reaches our area is very low confidence and depends on 
how thunderstorms evolve to our north or atop the boundary 
itself. There appear to be scenarios ranging with cooling relief
arriving as early as 10 AM to noon along the Lake Michigan 
shoreline (via storms developing over the lake this morning) to 
relief being delayed to the 4 to 6 PM time window (coverage of 
storms is minimized to our north/northeast). Ultimately, this is
something we won't be able to pin down until thunderstorms 
actually develop. Note that areas away from the Wisconsin state 
line and Lake Michigan shoreline (I-80 south) will bake in the 
heat today regardless. 

Even with the potential for an earlier arrival time for relief 
to arrive today, there still looks to be a window for heat index
values to reach the 100 to 105F range for a majority of the 
area. All things considered, felt the course of least regret 
was to alter the inherited headlines rather than punting to the 
day shift giving them an essentially zero lead time scenario. 
So, went ahead and expanded the heat advisory for all but Lake 
County IL. For Cook County in particular, today will be the 
third day in a row with a peak heat index in excess of 100 
degrees. When paired with warm overnight low temperatures (heat 
index remaining above 80F), had no choice but to upgrade to an 
Extreme Heat Warning for prolonged impacts of dangerous heat 
within the urban heat island. Again, do expect relief to arrive 
at some point this afternoon/evening particularly along the 
Wisconsin state line and the Lake Michigan shoreline, just when
is the primary question.

Finally, if thunderstorms do develop in our area this 
afternoon, the very moist airmass will support hefty water- 
loaded downdrafts and subsequent localized cold pool 
amalgamation to encourage the development of clusters with a 
threat for locally damaging winds. 


Tonight into Friday...

Ensemble model guidance is in fair agreement that an upper- 
level short-wavelength tough in the northern Plains will 
propagate toward the central Great Lakes tonight as the 
orientation of the upper-level height gradient bends anti-
cyclonically into quasi- northwesterly flow. While low-level 
flow and ascent ahead of the feature does not look particularly 
strong, CAM-based guidance is insistent in vigorous renewed 
thunderstorm development on the cool side of the composite 
outflow boundary ahead of a southeastward-racing complex of 
storms from the northern Plains. Southeasterly storm motions
